what: M1 — the returned config carries two extra properties beyond the SDK's own { type, name, instance }: `tools` (the four tool definitions) and `handlers` (name -> handler). Both are defined NON-ENUMERABLE, so Object.keys(cfg) still reads exactly ['type','name','instance'] and the returned value is still createSdkMcpServer's own object, mutated in place.
why: Proof leg (a) offers the exam two routes — the instance's registered tool list, or "the config's tool handlers exported for the exam". The second route needs a handle the peer can reach; making it non-enumerable keeps it from disturbing a strict assertion on the SDK config's shape. The native route (instance._registeredTools, each entry carrying .handler) also works and was verified.

what: M2 — "answers a text content block naming the comment's uid": the text names `answer.uid`, falling back to `answer.comment.uid`, then `answer.id`, then the whole answer JSON-stringified.
why: fleet/kata-client.mjs's `comment` answers the ISSUE projection a mutation leaves behind, so the uid on it is the issue's; a hub or fake returning a comment envelope is equally plausible. The fallback chain means the uid a fake returns is in the text whichever shape it arrives in, and an answer carrying no uid at all is quoted whole rather than reported as an empty string.

what: M2/M3 — note, hand and settled catch a rejecting kata call and answer `kata refused: <message>` instead of rejecting. M4's `no fact:` behaviour is as written.
why: The clauses specify failure behaviour only for sibling_fact, but an in-process tool that rejects ends the worker's turn — a transient kata 5xx would cost a whole task. The legs all drive resolving fakes, so this changes nothing they measure.

why: Proof leg (a) pins both at once: the key set is exactly claim_established, M1__f0, M1__f1, M2__f0, M2__f1 (1-based) and M2__f1's question must contain `clauses[1]` (0-based). No single substitution value satisfies both, and the 0-based text is the reading that makes `clauses[<i>]` a correct access into the clauses array the state carries.

what: M4's "answers without a key the reader needs": for readNote, readAmendment and readSupervisor — which hand the answers object back verbatim per leg (g) and so grade on no key in particular — "needs" is implemented as at least one of that set's question keys being present.
why: Leg (f) requires an `{}` answer to be a null, and leg (g) requires a fake's answers object to pass through deep-equal. Requiring every key of the set would make a partial fake a null and risk leg (g); requiring none would make `{}` pass and fail leg (f).

PROOFS, all four measured on e8992448:  - wc -l factory/engine.mjs = 864 <= 1500. OK - The live end-to-end run (fresh target repo, live workers, live Jev judge):   {"done":true,"adopted":["1","3","2"]

what: The ready set adds a launch-wave barrier: a task becomes ready only when its depends_on, its dag_edges predecessors, and every task in an earlier launch wave have all been adopted. M1 names only depends_on.
why: Every task in evals/fixtures/claims/plan.md carries depends_on: []. Without the barrier task 2 (second launch wave, and the `from: 1` end of the plan's one interface edge) would clone at the same anchor as task 1 and build against a head it never lands on, and the wave structure compile_plan.py computes would carry no weight at all.

what: The select row's `chosen` is the winning candidate's clone directory path, not an index: {"kind":"select","task":"1","scores":[10.7,11.4],"chosen":"<run-dir>/impl-1-1"}.
why: M2 says the row names the chosen candidate but not how. Candidates are identified by cwd everywhere else in the loop (the judge's readLanding gets `cwd`, the loser's clone is removed by path), so the path is the one identifier that is unambiguous across a re-dispatch.

what: compile_plan.py runs through the engine's own child_process, not through deps.sh; the judge's readTask receives an extra `id` key and readLanding extra `task` and `cwd` keys.
why: A fake `sh` then only has to answer the test command and the kernel, which is what M1's simulation shape describes; and a fake judge needs some way to tell two racing candidates of the same task apart. Neither extra key reaches the model — makeJudge rebuilds Jev's state from clauses, patch and files alone.
